segments.description: Welcome coaches to the Grand Slam Coaches Conference and thank you again for tuning into our final locker room Q&A session for the conference. This session we have the pleasure of Jeff Coates his company. He joined the ATP Pro Circuit in 1996 was a very accomplished doubles player. He had many years of success on the tour when he multiple doubles titles had a career high ranking of 11 in the world represented his country and Davis Cup just to highlight a few of his accomplishments. He then made the transition from player to coach in 2013 and teamed up with as coach with former number one doubles pairing Robert Farah and Julian Sebastian Cabal, helping them win the 2019 Wimbledon and US Open titles. That's a fair resume Jeff. Welcome. Thank you for your time. I know that you're very busy down at the AO at the moment with your cohort of players so we very much appreciate you joining us today. Yeah, thanks thanks for having me Brett much appreciated. I love your presentation. I'd like to kick things off if you don't mind by just starting with the early years out on the tennis court for you, what that looked like back home and perhaps how that forged a foundation of the success that you had on the tennis court. I think that the way I grew up was a little bit different to most. I come from a family you know with eight siblings so I basically had to, you know backyard, you made our own racket of wood, and then I took the orange bags to two poles and drew a court where it's sort of a gravel background there so that's how I started, you know it's

your normal where you join a club where you go to school or something so that was my introduction to tennis. You know, we used to, we used to play and we played I think for a liter of coke or something so I was always the youngest. I lost pretty much all the time, crying, and I couldn't take it anymore. But I think if I go back and I think it, it taught me the mental side of things because my brothers always used to beat me, but just to grab in those background it made me, I think a little bit tougher, you know and then. Obviously it was tough in the beginning back in South Africa during apartheid era so I wasn't allowed to play tournaments so that made it also tough I obviously didn't know why at the time. And then once I got sort of playing my first tournament I remember it's weird. I got five hours from Cape Town. So my brother took me. And then, once I was allowed to play. And then I lost my first semi final against actually somebody that was one in the country and I'm like, I didn't like that feeling at all. And my brother said well that happens when you only practice twice a week I'm like okay I'll give it a shot. Let me practice every day and see what happens and I ended up beating the guy pretty convincingly and then. So from there the Federation saw me I moved to Johannesburg at age 12 away from the family, and then on a Monday Wednesday Fridays, I had coaching at the Federation and on a Tuesday first I kind of had to do my own thing.

And which I did, but it taught me a lot of discipline, a lot of different things. Yeah, I moved at the age of 16 I moved to America actually went to John Newcombe Tennis Academy there for two years which I absolutely enjoyed, and then turn pro in 96. So yeah, so yeah I think, overall, it really made me tough I was one of the best South Africans in as a junior so yeah, they're all good. Yeah, number one up until the 18. Yeah, I was one in my age group I only lost my first match in my age group at age 18. So, yeah, I don't know if I still have the record or something but yeah, I don't know if it's a good thing or not. I think it's it's good to have a bit of a ratio between winning and losing. Now that I'm a coach I realized it was good but also not that good for my needed more and more competition although I went up an age group and then I became one under 16 and 18 at the same time. But the better kids I say would say the top five in the country they now went to play junior woman and all that stuff so I didn't really get to play against them which would have been nice. A product called home court tennis that we rolled out through lockdowns here in Australia and sounds very similar in design to your experiences as a youngster where it's really promoting kind of that unstructured play and play at home and exploration. Do you attribute that to the successes later on. No 100%. I mean, if I if I look back and especially with what we had two years ago with the covert. It kind of brought me back to roots and I worked out some stuff for the Federation as well we just go back to the wall.

I mean, you can't get better than the wall so that's what I did a lot on a Sunday afternoon and Saturday afternoons against the wall. Bless my mom, you know, she she couldn't sleep at the time because she wanted to take an afternoon nap and here I am doing volleys and hitting against the wall and I would get frustrated because my brother would say you have to make you do like a little circle. Like a hundred in a row if not you start back to zero even if you must at 99 so that's what I did. So I'm a person if I if I can't get it I won't stop until I do get 100. So yeah, definitely helped. Yeah. How much doubles did you play as a youngster. I know here in this country juniors don't tend to play as much doubles and there's not that same emphasis and glitz and glamour associated with the doubles in that in those junior years. So how much doubles did you play as a kid. I mean we don't. When we decide to play tennis we don't go into okay I want to be a doubles player or something we obviously you play singles you play and I was lucky enough that I played enough singles that my brother also said, let's use doubles for your singles because in doubles you have to now make. And he was not even a coach he just played the game and said, I think it's good for you to play doubles because if you want to have a good return in singles that the court is smaller and now you play singles the court becomes bigger.

You have to learn how to make first serves and certain spots where in singles you can chip to return back in the middle of the court and the rally starts you know sometimes you can do that. But in doubles is a little different so I was lucky enough that I learned a lot from a young age being so young and playing with with my older brothers and people that were a lot older than me double so I learned a different craftsmanship to different there was a different kind of playing the little things the little lobs and all those things I think later on maybe it helped me. And, and I did the same when I grew up in Johannesburg on a Saturday morning and a Sunday morning I had league matches. And that's what happened when I played league match and I absolutely enjoyed it. I mean, we used to call them like sort of old old bullies old guys. And when they love you like how the, how does this guy love me you know and it was fun and look how I think that I would mean my, my friend my doubles partner was just to absolutely love when they hit a little slow angle pass you or they bring you in and then they love you like wow, you know they really play smart and don't just hit it like we used to. I think I learned a lot in those young years and just like yeah I think in South Africa that's something that has changed. We're actually trying to bring it a lot more back in South Africa to play a lot more doubles tournaments because that will also help you especially you know if you play whether you're going to play one day to pick up you play college, whatever there's always going to be double

BJK Cup it's always going to be helpful schools matches and stuff so I think it's a great game. It's great to socialize with and just it's just fun, you know, you can really really learn a lot from it. Yeah, and you, you touched on the fun aspect right there at the end and the social element to it because tennis in a singles environment in that fishbowl can be quite daunting. So how does the fun come out or how did the fun come out for you as a youngster on the tennis court playing doubles. I mean I just enjoyed competing I always felt like you have if you play doubles there's four personalities on the court and how they get you know it's all about that chemistry. You know when you play doubles it's like a marriage if it's not there it's not there you got to find a way to sort of work with that chemistry and you know when you play club matches or whether you play junior tennis I just think it's a great game. And, and that's what it should be like at the end of the day as you become professional yes it becomes tougher. But at the end of the day you're going to ask yourself why did I start in the first place you play because you love it. And I think if we can sort of balance that even now I'm trying to sort of. What was my guys warm up I tried to bring sort of fun things in and towards the end finisher you start with something fun and you end with something fun. So that's what I'm trying to get in and obviously in between you work hard but then at the end of the weather it's reflexes at the end make it fun and I like to still get involved as well and I, and I would be like all right if you get to hit me I'll do 20 push ups.

And kind of makes it interesting or you do one court sprint you always trying, you know, bring some sort of element of fun into it, and teaching these kids at the same time and I say kids but they're like 28 29 years old you know but still I just don't want to be the coach that just teaches the tennis I want to teach them some life lessons as well. Yeah, and I imagine to the adjustment in geometry of the play space from doubles to singles or vice versa from singles to doubles just offers an array of exploration of different strokes, different ways to play the game a different tempo, how to bring in and utilize your partner. So is that something that you bring out onto the tennis court when you're training with your junior kids. No 100%. I mean it's just for them to understand first the basic elements of the geometry of the court as well. It's like that person is there and and these are your options. So you've able to teach them do some little different drills on on on the court. And, and just to understand that what shot is a more percentage shot than the other shot. And I think it's once they understand that but what I see a lot these days is kids just hit for the sake of hitting, you know and and and and especially even more so doubles. It's a game of mistakes you're not going to get that many winners so how do you force the mistake how do you find little gaps to maybe open up and see where there's an open space to maybe be able to hit a winner, which is not obviously that easy.

You can get older and stuff you can set asus you can do return winners but how often does that happen compared to forcing your opponent to make a mistake whether it's in in junior tennis where it's league matches where it's pro level and and obviously at this level it just becomes more and more complicated and the margins becomes just so much smaller, but if you can teach them at a younger age that they as you grow up the margins become smaller it's like in life, you know, it's easy when you're kid. You just don't worry about anything moment that pays the both and later on everything becomes a little different so I think it's if you can teach these kids something at a young age. That will be definitely helpful. Yeah, and I guess with that in mind, referring specifically to some of the stuff that you talked about in your presentation around formations. We don't see a lot of different formations, particularly out on a junior doubles court here in Australia, you know, for the purposes of challenging the turn it to change the angle and getting the return out of their rhythm and getting that feel of being uncomfortable. Is that something that you really encourage at that junior level to go out there and explores that uncomfortable feeling of being in a different formation, different position to invoke a different response to the match. I like to do it, to be honest, and I've been asked a few times at home, even at schools and stuff to be able to show some double strolls and stuff and I like to ask the players themselves.

If I stand there and I like to be on court and showing them if I stand there that person hit the shot, for example, up to T, which areas can I cover. So obviously I trust my partner surf and then I stick out the record I'm like you see these are the option that this person can beat you with. So you got to make that gap at least smaller in the middle you don't want everything just to kind of go through the middle and play normal when you play I formation. That's why it's there because now you're giving the player sort of a different look because if you have somebody that returns really well cross court. Well I formation is probably one way to take that away from the from the opponent just a little bit, and the adjustment really becomes where you do the I formation it becomes on the net person where they stand some people like to stand in the one block some people stand in the middle between the line where the line is between you know sort of that. So it just depends if you see that person still beating you cross court, especially when you serve tea. Either way on the news or the ad, then you just adjust. I mean I'm always like one to kind of adjust my stance where I am and I and I and I dare that return I'm taking that completely away today you're not beating me, but with that comes another you sort of give up the middle. If he if that person then does hit the middle because that's why you're not taking away but now you're also taking away the person strength by not beating you safe to hit a late return in the trams for

example, and that you if they take on hitting consistently then you obviously know when you surf tea they like it. So you take that away completely as where you start so I think it's where people don't want to do it because they don't really know how to do it, or and some we don't really explain it well enough. So I feel like you be able to do it well, you need to explain it well enough and you're able to show them on on on the court and maybe sometimes a lot of players visual players I like to see things. So it's, it's easier for sometimes easier for us to explain, but it's sometimes easier for them to see it themselves. Fantastic. We've just had a question come in from Scott Rawlins. How much data do you use when looking at strengths and weaknesses of the players that you're working with. I'm especially in the beginning. If I start with players, I do it a lot and getting to know trying to get as much data as possible. Once I get to know my players and their opponents I have a sort of a whole data and stuff that I go on with. I'm one person that likes it but I don't like over like it. You know I feel like if it's too much information also. Again, it depends on the player you coaching. Like when I was with Cabal and Farah the one guy for it doesn't like it too much. Let's just give me one or two things and that's it. The other guy's okay I can give him ABCD doesn't matter. He'll just process it and it works for him. So again it all depends. I think it's great for coaches to have it. The one thing that I really enjoyed was the 80 cup when I was an African for the coach captain a few years ago, where we can actually go into the strategy room and actually show them.

So being with with Lord Harris on the court, you could show actually what way serving and all those things, even though even in doubles you can say hey man this guy's doing this and you need to serve more there because he's covering whether that's like now on demand that I think maybe may not be happening in the near future because a lot of other sports have it already. And I guess just on that that subject. If you were to crystal ball. What the the next 1020 years of in the future doubles tennis looks like is the ATP cup and tapping into that live data is that is that an insight into a view into the future. I would think so. I've definitely think so I know like for example, on the, the wj to have the coaching already whether singles or doubles to have it on court and where the men is, we don't want to be sort of on court, they I know with the ATP coaches to the meetings we've had. I do want to bring it in. I know they really trying it and they sort of this playing around with it. I definitely think that is something in the future for for our game. Another sport has it. So it's just us with a, how are we going to get there but this is definitely the ATP cup is something they, they playing around with and I think definitely in the future that's, look, that's going to be the way forward. That's what I think, you know, with a lot of data and a lot of things you can do and at the end of the day you can say yeah but you give this one more.

You still have to execute you still have to make this serve you still have to, if you're gonna cross and you tell them the cross still has to be perfect timing because that's all about timing. So, I think we're just going to have to get used to that in the future. Yeah, interesting time will tell. We have another question coming in from Jay who asks. How early would you teach young players different formations. Do you teach them all start what do you get the basics and then say at a green stage level start introducing things like I formation. Yeah, I would probably just do the basics first. And then I would do a little bit because once you sort of fast, the green phase, then maybe bring that in. Again, it depends on the on the player itself, your sort of structure. Like you want to be able to get the players to love the game and have fun with it by introducing them because sometimes they like to have a partner I know my daughter that's nine. She loves it just because she has a best friend with her and, and when daddy comes home. I, she likes to play against me, you know with me and another person for example and we rotate in threes, and then I'll tell them okay I stand here but I do this so I bring it in sort of in a fun element and then I'll tell her to serve sort of in the block we just play in the four blocks and I'm gonna stand here but look what daddy can do this way I can do that way, sort of and then I tell her to do that.

Maybe fake you and you maybe, but you do it in a sort of a fun way. So they enjoy that and, and, and, but I don't know if she likes Dennis that much, but I try and make it fun for her. When you're working with pharaoh and cabal, we started there outside the top 60, ultimately got them to wall number one. Can you share with us a little bit of what that looked like both on and off the court to elevate them to that that number one status. Yeah, I think what it looked like I was like what did I get myself involved here. I'm like, I don't know. I couldn't believe that's like man, I wish I was still playing because I was, I was still sort of really fairly active at the time, while I'm still them. And when I said to them, and I sat down with them I said guys it's almost like you are two guys playing doubles but you just stop singles a while ago, but you're still playing the same way. So which way do you want to play so I was trying to get them to be sort of hybrids where they, they serve and state back a lot obviously growing up in South America. And I'm like, if we do this together and then same thing. I like in the beginning I did a lot of threes with them where I would rotate with them I would be in one corner only, and then they two up at the net and then we would rotate where one guys in the net to at the back we would kind of do those a lot, just to kind of just for them to understand what the geometry of the court can be like in different ways and now you only have to kind of play in one corner for example and you, like I said earlier on, it's a game of mistakes and we play a game where you're not allowed to hit a winner

and you have to force the person to make a mistake. So you get to go so in the beginning it was tough, because it took a little bit time, but once they understood what I was trying to do and they had all the trust and believe in me. It worked out and then it was just a matter of staying healthy unfortunately Rob was, I think the first three years I was either back the neck or the wrist. So, and I said to him, you know, something we need to change is you you four months out of the year for the last three years. And we still like sort of the 11th 10th team I said top eight is just around the corner to stay healthy for me for four months but in terms you have to change your, your diet nutrition we need to do this because I would need to maximize how I push you. And so we did some blood tests and everything. And that was a big change because now I could kind of do whatever I want with them and push them as hard as I can but I would say the probably one of the biggest change for for because before winning I think the third round was the best at Wimbledon. So, and we always lost to guys that sort of grass court players but lost close matches and I said, These are the things that I picked up over the last two three years. And I think for us to change we need to start working on a few different things and which I did already kind of in the beginning of the year, because I didn't want to start the grass court season now working on those things.

Every day, I would take them individually but I would spend a half an hour with each one of them on the return lab and the chip return, just to kind of get into the point which something they didn't really have. So I would work a lot on that. And I think that's probably one of the reasons we won Wimbledon because we were just in play a lot more than before. They would take to 3040 and now they would serve Rob to the T and they would constantly miss because his better return was cross court like we talked earlier on, guys got smart by standing a little bit more over now that gap becomes a lot smaller for him cross court, and he can't really pull it up up the line that well, then sort of in the middle, and then they still put the ball away and on grass it's easy just just a ball and it just dies. So I had to come up with something different for him to be able to chip as an alternative and that works kind of gives him another option or two. Yeah, that's brilliant. I suggested in his doubles presentation earlier this week that there's perhaps a downtrend or he's is seeing a downtrend in Sir Volley on the pro tour at the moment. What are your thoughts. I think it the way it obviously with a lot of the singles guys are there but I'm still a firm believer if especially in a court like how Australian open places here. If you hit your spot say a meter or even meeting a half from the baseline, and you stick it pretty decent, and you have two guys at the net. Ultimately, I feel the chances of two guys at the net will still do the guys at the baseline.

That's how I feel because if you if you value that good and you just do normal drills. Again, we're talking about there's not a lot of gaps there so if you keep on forcing your opponent, especially two guys staying back the volume was likely would have the chance to to to still win only downside of this. So how the volley becomes short or the guys start hitting well and it's not a great volley then yeah it becomes 50 50 or something, but the pressure. I think it's more for the baseline. If, if the volume is volley well enough like you would probably see a lot of the top teams does. But yeah, I think it's just probably a mix of things but definitely heading more that way than what it used to be. I'm going to answer one next question. One up one back to back to at the net. What's the most successful doubles situation. I think you've covered that one. I think it's again it's the preference the preference but I again if you up to statistically I think if you do up at the at the net and you play a lot of the guys especially like the singles guys that likes to be back. You have the option of kind of volley sort of relatively deep and the next one if you if somebody has like a ball had great hands I would always tell him why don't you probably one deep and one drop should use your hands more. You forced the your opponent that's not as comfortable at the net and you want to bring them to the net and that's one way of doing it.

Coach the, you can put coach the person first before you coach the player. Yeah, and then the clay court season start again so yeah I'm looking forward to the next few months as well because it's a different challenges I love challenges and I'm really looking forward to figuring out those challenges you know sometimes you, sometimes you get thrown into into the dark and sometimes in the beginning everything works your way but unfortunately my side now with the injuries and stuff with the guys. Thank you so much for being with us today and for putting your presentation together.
